lede: The same order, written by the brotherhoods and copied by their enemies. Each page sets the passages next to each other, in English; every passage links to its place in the texts, with the original beside it.

pairs.frage: Vyšehrad 1420 and Lipany 1434: one shout, two outcomes.
pairs.note: Below Vyšehrad the Praguers were already fleeing when someone shouted 'fugiunt, fugiunt!', and the rush that followed won the battle. At Lipany the lords pretended to flee; the brethren shouted the same words, left their wagons to pursue, and could not get back into them. Between the two days stands the ordinance's fifth article: no troop shall break away from its order.

Below Vyšehrad the peasants' flails took no prisoners, and the Hussite nobles saved what enemy lords they could, for ransom and for their rank. Three years later the ordinance makes every capture common property, to be shared by elders of every estate. The imperial diet gives each prisoner to the lord who paid for the man who took him. The difference in what a prisoner was worth, and to whom, runs through the whole war.

pairs.frage: The first demand of both orders.
pairs.note: Žižka's brotherhood asks for 'orderly obedience' because disobedience has cost it men and goods. Three years later the electors at Nuremberg ask for obedience to the captains, and the Frankfurt diet for obedience 'without any contradiction', 'no one excepted', in the ordinance's own phrase. What the crusade must add is the clause that no lord shall shield his own man.

pairs.frage: The march, the camp and the fire.
pairs.note: The ordinance keeps every troop under its banner and reserves burning to those appointed to it. The Frankfurt diet forbids foraging, burning and breaking camp 'unless the banner sent for it is with them', and adds the order to run or to stand. The rule the field armies broke at Lipany is the rule the crusade copied from them.

Here the orders part. The ordinance has all booty brought to one place and shared among rich and poor by elders chosen from every estate, peasants included; whoever keeps anything dies like Achan. The crusade shares food in equal parts, leaves captured places to the captains, and gives each prisoner, with his ransom, to the lord who paid for the man who took him.

pairs.frage: Who may not be in the camp.
pairs.note: Both orders clear the camp of dice-players and harlots and punish those who curse. The ordinance threatens banishment or death 'according to God's law'; the electors and the diet name the pillory, the whip and the hand.

pairs.frage: Desertion, the token and the wagon.
pairs.note: No one leaves the field army without the elders' leave and a sure token; whoever does is a 'faithless thief' of God's cause. The Frankfurt diet denies safe conduct to any lord who rides home without the captains' token; the Silesian wagon order binds its eighteen men to their wagon unless the captain commands otherwise.

pairs.frage: A threshing tool becomes a weapon.
pairs.note: A Moravian lord tells Sigismund before Vyšehrad that he fears the peasants' flails. At Beroun the chronicler calls a troop simply 'the flailmen'. Seven years later the imperial diet writes flails into its own wagon order: two flailmen to each war wagon.

pairs.frage: What the brethren shared, and what they collected.
pairs.note: In September 1420 Tábor's bishop is charged with giving out the community's money 'according to each brother's need'; in October Tábor collects from the peasants the rents its priests had said were no longer owed. The ordinance of 1423 shares the booty 'among the rich and the poor as is befitting'. Sharing and exacting stand side by side from the beginning.

Bohemia counts the wagons, guns, money and banners the crusaders left as God's gift to her men. The cardinal counts the same things as loss, and adds what his own soldiers carried off: the war chest collected in Germany for the pope. The ordinance had made all booty common and its theft a crime against God; the imperial order had given each man's plunder to his lord.

pairs.frage: A concession in a poem, a submission after a battle.
pairs.note: In the Domažlice song of 1431 the cardinal advises granting three of the Four Articles and the pope agrees, provided the fourth, the church's property, is passed over in silence. Three years later the field armies' captains, beaten at Lipany, bind themselves to whatever the lords and towns decide at Prague. The Compacts of 1436 granted, in substance, what the poem's cardinal had proposed.

pairs.frage: Indulgence, own cost and common booty.
pairs.note: The pope pays the crusade in grace: full remission for those who fight at their own cost or pay a fighter, sixty days for the poor who can only fast and pray, and a share by the size of the gift. The imperial diet makes every man march at his own cost and pay for his food. The brotherhood pays itself from what it takes, pooled and shared by elders of every estate.

pairs.frage: The same crime, charged and absolved.
pairs.note: The bull's charge against the Hussites is that they burn churches, monasteries and images and rage against priests. Laurence of Březová records the Taborites doing so, and Žižka burning thirty-seven priests and monks at Beroun. The same bull empowers the legate's confessors to absolve crusaders who have laid hands on clergy or been arsonists and committers of sacrilege.

pairs.frage: The article on public sins, in the field and at Basel.
pairs.note: The brotherhood's ordinance gives the power to punish to 'brother Žižka and the communities': banishment, flogging, beheading, hanging, burning, drowning, by God's law and with no person excepted. The Compacts accept the article that public sins must be punished, and take the punishing away from everyone without a lawful court.

pairs.frage: The church's property: silence, then affirmation.
pairs.note: In the Domažlice song the pope grants three articles and orders silence on the fourth, because the church's authority rests on its wealth. Two years later the council's legates do not keep silent: they declare that the church may own houses, villages, towns, castles and cities, and that its goods must not be held by others. The bull of 1421 had already put the crusaders' goods under St Peter's protection.
